title: A Man's Brother Gives Him Up
intro: One of Abu al-Atahiya's poems of renunciation (zuhd), in a short, quick metre; the sources do not say when or why he wrote it. It opens with the thought that even a man's brother and father cannot keep death from him, then plays out his deathbed and funeral almost entirely in the commands of the people around him: ask him, prompt him, wash him, shroud him, carry him, bury him, until they walk away as if they had never known him. It turns next to people at large, who build what they never live in and gather what they never use, honour those they need and shun those who need them, and it ends on the refusal to beg and on the friend who is a brother only while you need nothing from him. The closing lines circulated on their own in the books of literary lore: al-Jahiz and Ibn Qutayba give the last two to Abu al-Atahiya, al-Abbasi says the philologist al-Asma'i admired them, and Ibn Abi al-Dunya records the final passage as a Bedouin of the tribe of Tamim recited it to him, without naming a poet.

translation: A man's brother gives him up
to death, and so does his father.
1.sharh: Even those closest to a man, his brother and his father, cannot keep death from him; when it comes, they give him up to it. The same verb, “give him up”, returns in line 18.

translation: The father of sons does not last,
and his sons do not last either.
2.sharh: Death takes the father who leaves sons behind, and then takes the sons too. No line of descent outlasts it, however long it runs.

translation: Many a man much spoken of by his people
went from among them, and they forgot him.
3.sharh: Many a man whose name was always on his people's lips was forgotten soon after death took him from among them. The fame people work for barely outlives them.

translation: When a man has used up his years,
his years have used him up.
4.sharh: A man spends his years, and in spending them is spent by them. The line uses one verb both ways, so the years do to him exactly what he did to them.

translation: And it is as if the man's nearest kin
are already weeping over him,
5.sharh: The poet pictures the man's last hour as if it had already come: his relatives are weeping over him. From here the poem plays out a deathbed and a funeral, step by step.

translation: and as if the people have stood up
and said, “Get to him.”
6.sharh: The people around him jump up and call to one another to reach him, as though something could still be done to save him.

translation: “Ask him, talk to him,
move him, prompt him.”
7.sharh: The commands come one after another without “and”, catching the rush and confusion around the bed: first they try to rouse him, then they help him to his last words.

translation: When the people have given up hope of him,
they say, “Turn him.”
8.sharh: Once they lose hope of saving him, they stop trying to rouse him and start preparing him for death, though he is still breathing. With “turn him”, they already treat him as one of the departed.

translation: “Turn him, turn his face,
stretch him out, close his eyes.”
9.sharh: The man they were talking to a moment ago is now handled as a body: turned, straightened, his eyes closed, as the Prophet closed the eyes of his companion Abu Salama, saying that the sight follows the soul when it is taken. The commands still come without “and”.

translation: “Hurry him on his journey;
hurry, don't hold him back.”
10.sharh: They hurry to get him out to the grave and urge one another not to delay. The Prophet told Muslims to make haste with a bier, but here the haste has a colder edge: the man they wept over is now a task to be done with.

translation: “Lift him, wash him,
shroud him, perfume him.”
11.sharh: Four commands in one line: he is lifted, washed, wrapped in a shroud and perfumed for the grave, like jobs done in a hurry.

translation: When he is wrapped in the shrouds,
they say, “Now carry him.”
12.sharh: Once he is wrapped in the shroud, all that is left is to carry him. The man who walked among them has become a load.

translation: “Take him out on the timbers of death,
walk with him to the grave.”
13.sharh: He is carried out on the bier, which the poet calls “the timbers of death”, and the mourners walk behind him to the grave.

translation: When they have prayed over him,
someone says, “Bring him, bury him.”
14.sharh: After the funeral prayer, the last thing they do for him, someone calls for him to be brought to the grave and buried without delay. The verb is impersonal, “it is said”, as if the whole crowd spoke.

translation: When they have entrusted him to the earth
as a pledge, they leave him.
15.sharh: They leave him in the earth like a deposit held in pledge, which will not be released. The word recalls the Quran's “every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned” (74:38).

translation: They leave him behind under heaped earth;
they load him, weigh him down.
16.sharh: They leave him under the heaped earth of the grave, weighing him down with it as one loads a pack animal. The body they carried on their shoulders now carries a load it will never put down.

translation: They send him off, put him far away,
leave him alone, set him apart.
17.sharh: Four verbs for one thing: sent away, put far off, left alone, set apart. The piling up makes the loneliness of the grave felt.

translation: They bid him farewell, part from him,
give him up, leave him behind.
18.sharh: They take their leave and go. “Give him up” is the verb the poem opened with: what his brother and father did then, everyone does now.

translation: They turn back from him and leave him
as if they had never known him,
19.sharh: They walk back from the grave and leave him, as if they had never known him, though they were his own people weeping over him an hour before.

translation: as if the people, in all he went through,
had never stood beside him.
20.sharh: It is as though they had never been his people at all, though they saw him through every stage from deathbed to grave; they return to their own affairs and he is forgotten.

translation: People build buildings
they never live in;
21.sharh: People build houses they will never live in, because death comes first and others move in. This opens three matching lines on what people strive for and never enjoy.

translation: people amass wealth
they never eat;
22.sharh: They gather wealth they never get to use; they die and leave it to others. “Eating” wealth is the Arabic way of saying enjoying it.

translation: people pursue hopes
they never reach.
23.sharh: And they chase hopes they never reach, because life is shorter than hope. The three lines share one pattern: people, what they strive for, and what they never get from it.

translation: Anyone who will not take people as his guide
is left behind by them.
24.sharh: People turn their backs on anyone who will not follow their ways and take them as his model. One manuscript reads it the other way round: anyone the people do not make their leader is left alone.

translation: The dead have travelled on to what
they sent ahead, and found it.
25.sharh: The dead have moved on to the deeds they sent ahead of them, and found them waiting. The line echoes the Quran: “whatever good you send ahead for yourselves, you will find it with God” (73:20).

translation: People's life is good, whatever it is,
if they are content with it.
26.sharh: Life is good, whatever kind of life it is, as long as people are content with it. Happiness lies in contentment, not in what one has.

translation: Live as you like: whoever is gladdened
by his world will be grieved by it.
27.sharh: Live as you please: the world never stays sweet for anyone. Whatever gladdens a man today will grieve him tomorrow, and the line sets the two verbs, gladden and grieve, side by side.

translation: If a man does not honour people,
they will not honour him.
28.sharh: Honour is returned in kind: a man who does not honour others will not be honoured by them. The same verb in both halves makes the exchange exact.

translation: Anyone people have no need of,
they belittle;
29.sharh: People think little of anyone they have no need of, however great his worth. Their measure is use, not merit.

translation: anyone people turn to with their requests,
they look up to.
30.sharh: And they look up to anyone they go to with requests. A man's standing depends on how much people need him, not on his merit.

translation: Whoever approaches his brother with wealth,
he is a brother to him;
31.sharh: A man who comes to his brother with money finds him a brother indeed; for most people, brotherhood follows wealth. The implication is that a true brother shows himself only in need.

translation: but if he looks to him,
he sees in him what hurts him.
32.sharh: But if he turns to him for help, he meets with coldness that hurts him. The version Ibn Abi al-Dunya heard spells it out: “if he is driven to need him”.

translation: A man is honoured, and if he grows poor,
his own sons push him away.
33.sharh: A man is honoured while he has money; when he grows poor, even his own sons, who owe him most, push him away.

translation: If people saw a prophet
begging, they would give him nothing,
34.sharh: People are so mean that if they saw a prophet begging they would give him nothing, let alone anyone less. Their meanness makes no distinction between one beggar and another.

translation: and they, if they craved
a dog's food, would eat it.
35.sharh: Yet they are so greedy that if they fancied a dog's food they would eat it. They refuse the noblest and stoop to the lowest.

translation: You will not see me, to the end of time,
open my mouth to ask.
36.sharh: He will never open his mouth to ask anyone for anything as long as he lives. Four lines follow in the diwan, telling the listener to ask God alone; the reciter leaves them out.

translation: Only those who have merit
are known for merit among people.
37.sharh: Merit is credited only to those who truly have it; it cannot be claimed or bought. Another version has “only those who have merit recognise it”.

translation: The best kindness is one
for which no face is cheapened.
38.sharh: The best kindness is the one given unasked, so that no one has to lower himself to request it. Asking costs the asker his dignity, the “water of his face”.

translation: As long as you can do without your friend,
you are his brother for ever;
39.sharh: As long as you need nothing from your friend, he treats you as a brother for ever. His affection lasts exactly as long as it costs him nothing. Ibn Qutayba quotes this pair straight after Jarir's “You are my brother as long as I have no need of you”.

translation: but when you need him for an hour,
his mouth spits you out.
40.sharh: But the moment you need him, even briefly, he spits you out like something he cannot stomach. Al-Abbasi records that al-Asma'i admired these two closing lines.

1.1.1.head: أَسلَمَ
1.1.1.meaning: Yuslimu: gives up, abandons someone to what befalls him. “The man” is its object.

1.2.1.head: المَنايا
1.2.1.meaning: Al-manaya: deaths, death as each person's fated end.

2.1.1-2.head: أَبو الأَبناء
2.1.1-2.meaning: “The father of sons”: any father, not the nickname of one man.

2.1.4.head: بَقِيَ
2.1.4.meaning: Yab-: the start of yabqa, “lasts”, which ends at the start of the second half. Many lines of this poem run a word across the break.

5.1.1-2.head: كَأَن بِالمَرء
5.1.1-2.meaning: “As if with the man”: an idiom that pictures something still to come as if it were already happening.

6.2.3.head: أَدرِك
6.2.3.meaning: Reach him: hurry to him before it is too late.

7.2.2.head: لَقِّن
7.2.2.meaning: Prompt him: say the profession of faith, “there is no god but God”, so that the dying man repeats it as his last words.

8.2.3.head: حَرِّف
8.2.3.meaning: Turn him aside, probably onto his side towards Mecca, as is done with the dying.

9.1.2.head: وَجِّه
9.1.2.meaning: Turn his face towards the qibla, the direction of Mecca.

11.2.2.head: حَنِّط
11.2.2.meaning: Put hanut on him: the blend of perfumes laid on a dead body and its shroud.

13.1.3.head: أَعواد
13.1.3.meaning: A'wa-: the start of a'wad, “timbers, pieces of wood”, completed by di at the start of the second half.

13.2.3.head: شَيِّع
13.2.3.meaning: Escort him: walk with the bier to the grave.

14.1.2-3.head: صَلّى عَلَيه
14.1.2-3.meaning: Prayed over him: said the funeral prayer, standing before the body with four cries of “God is greatest” and prayers for the dead, without bowing or prostrating.

14.2.2.head: هاتِ
14.2.2.meaning: Bring, hand over; here, bring him to the grave.

15.2.2.head: رَهن
15.2.2.meaning: Rahn: a pledge, security left with a creditor.

16.1.3.head: رَدم
16.1.3.meaning: Radm: earth and stones heaped up to fill a gap; here, the earth of the grave.

16.2.1.head: أَوقَرَ
16.2.1.meaning: Awqara: to load with a wiqr, a heavy burden.

17.1.2.head: أَسحَقَ
17.1.2.meaning: Ashaqa: to put far away, from suhq, remoteness.

18.1.1.head: وَدَّعَ
18.1.1.meaning: Bid him farewell, as one sees off a traveller; line 10 has already called his last journey a departure.

20.2.4.head: وَلِيَ
20.2.4.meaning: From waliya: to be near someone, or to take charge of his affairs.

25.1.1.meaning: Have moved on, as a desert tribe breaks camp and travels.

30.1.3.meaning: Raghiba ila: to turn to someone with a request. With fi, the same verb means to desire.

31.2.1.head: الغِنى
31.2.1.meaning: Al-ghina: wealth, not to be confused with ghina', singing.

32.2.1.head: رَأى
32.2.1.meaning: Yar'a: “he sees”, a form of the verb that keeps its hamza, which the metre needs here.

33.1.4.head: أَملَقَ
33.1.4.meaning: Am-: the start of amlaqa, “became poor”, completed by laqa at the start of the second half.

35.1.2.meaning: “If”. Shukri Faisal's edition has law, “if (it were the case that)”; the reciter's in is the reading Ibn Abi al-Dunya gives.

36.2.2.head: تَسآل
36.2.2.meaning: Tas'al: asking, in a form that suggests asking again and again.

38.1.2.head: المَعروف
38.1.2.meaning: Al-ma'ruf: a kindness, a good turn done for someone.

38.2.1.head: اِبتَذَلَ
38.2.1.meaning: Cheapened: worn out like clothes kept for everyday work.

40.2.1.meaning: An hour: a short while, not sixty minutes.

40.2.2-3.head: مَجَّكَ فوه
40.2.2-3.meaning: Majja: to spit a liquid out of the mouth.
